title: The Scientist Who Discovered Electricity
description: Nobody discovered electricity alone - but one poor bookbinder's apprentice worked out how to make it, move it and understand it. This is the story of Michael Faraday, told in 3D animation.

shots.line: Every light you have ever switched on, every phone you have ever charged, every train, fridge and hospital machine, depends on one simple trick.
It's a trick so simple you could do it with a magnet and a coil of wire.
Without it there would be no electric light, no internet, and almost none of modern medicine.
And it was found by a poor bookbinder's boy who left school at thirteen, and never learned advanced mathematics.
His name was Michael Faraday. And this is how he turned electricity from a party trick into the power that runs the world.
People had seen electricity for thousands of years.
Around six hundred B.C., Greek thinkers noticed that rubbed amber could pick up feathers and bits of dust.
The Greek word for amber was elektron.
In sixteen hundred, the English physician William Gilbert borrowed it to coin a new Latin word, electricus.
In seventeen fifty two, Benjamin Franklin flew a kite into a storm, and showed that lightning was electricity too.
Franklin went on to invent the lightning rod, a simple metal spike that gives lightning a safe path into the ground.
Then in eighteen hundred, Alessandro Volta stacked discs of zinc and copper, separated by cloth soaked in salt water.
It was the first battery: a steady flow of electric current.
It was so important that the unit of electrical pressure, the volt, is named after him.
But it was weak, expensive, and nobody really understood what it was.
Electricity was a curiosity for lecture halls. A show, not a power source.
Michael Faraday was born in seventeen ninety one, near London, the son of a blacksmith.
His family was poor. At times he had a single loaf of bread to last him a week.
At fourteen, he became an apprentice to a bookbinder.
And instead of just binding the books, he read them.
His master, George Riebau, encouraged him, and even let him use the shop for experiments.
At night he went to lectures at a small club called the City Philosophical Society, where he learned chemistry, and how to explain science to an audience.
One of them was an encyclopedia, with a long article on electricity.
He built his own simple electrical machines from scraps, in the back of the shop.
In eighteen twelve, a customer gave him tickets to hear the most famous chemist in Britain, Sir Humphry Davy, at the Royal Institution.
Davy was a celebrity. Using huge batteries, he had discovered new elements, including sodium and potassium.
Crowds were so big that the street outside the Royal Institution is said to have become London's first one-way street.
Faraday took careful notes, rewrote them neatly, and bound them into a book.
Then he sent it to Davy, and asked him for a job.
Davy had recently been hurt in a laboratory explosion that damaged his eyesight, and for a short time, Faraday helped him as a secretary.
A few months later, one of Davy's lab assistants was sacked after a fight. And Davy hired Faraday to wash bottles.
Faraday worked his way up. He travelled across Europe with Davy, sometimes treated like a servant, but meeting the greatest scientists of the age.
shots.chapter: The assistant who outgrew his master

shots.line: In Paris they met André-Marie Ampère. In Italy, Faraday met Alessandro Volta himself.
In Florence, they used a giant magnifying glass to focus sunlight on a diamond, and burned it, proving that diamond is made of carbon.
Then, in eighteen twenty, the Danish scientist Hans Christian Oersted noticed something strange.
A wire carrying electric current made a nearby compass needle swing.
Electricity could create magnetism. The scientific world went wild.
In eighteen twenty one, Faraday built a small device: a wire dangling into a cup of mercury, beside an upright magnet.
When current flowed, the wire spun round and round the magnet.
Electricity had been turned into continuous motion. It was the ancestor of every electric motor.
He was so excited that he danced around the laboratory table with his brother-in-law.
That same year he married Sarah Barnard. They were together for forty six years.
But instead of praise, Faraday faced suspicion. Some, including Davy, felt he had used another scientist's ideas without giving credit.
It hurt him deeply.
Faraday became convinced of something.
If electricity could make magnetism, then surely magnetism could make electricity.
For years he tried. He put magnets next to wires. Nothing.
He wound wires around magnets. Nothing.
Between other work, he liquefied chlorine gas and discovered a new chemical called benzene. But the magnet problem would not go away.
In eighteen twenty four, he was elected to the Royal Society, reportedly against Davy's wishes. A year later, he was running the Royal Institution's laboratory.
Then, on the twenty ninth of August, eighteen thirty one, he took an iron ring, and wrapped two separate coils of wire around it.
One coil was connected to a battery. The other was connected to a needle that could detect current.
When he connected the battery, the needle jumped... and then fell back to zero.
When he disconnected it, the needle jumped the other way.
The current only appeared when the magnetism was changing.
Weeks later, he pushed a bar magnet into a coil of wire. The needle moved.
He pulled it out. The needle moved the other way.
Moving magnets make electricity. This is called electromagnetic induction.
He wrote down every experiment in numbered paragraphs. By the end of his life, his notebooks held more than sixteen thousand entries.
And it is the trick behind nearly every power station on Earth.
Faraday then spun a copper disc between the poles of a magnet.
A steady current flowed out of it, for as long as the disc kept turning.
It was the first electric generator. Turn something, and you get electricity.
Within a year, a French instrument maker, Hippolyte Pixii, built a hand-cranked generator using Faraday's principle.
It didn't matter what did the turning: falling water, steam, wind, or later, the heat from nuclear reactions.
Today almost all the electricity we use comes from Faraday's idea: magnets and coils of wire, moving past each other in giant generators.
Faraday couldn't do advanced maths. So he pictured what he couldn't calculate.
He sprinkled iron filings around magnets, and watched them snap into curved patterns.
He believed these lines of force were real things, filling the space around every magnet and every current.
Most scientists thought this was childish. But a young Scottish physicist, James Clerk Maxwell, turned Faraday's pictures into mathematics.
His equations showed something astonishing: light itself is a wave of electricity and magnetism.
Faraday had already shown, in eighteen forty five, that a magnet could twist a beam of light. It was a clue that light and magnetism were connected.
Radio, television, Wi-Fi and mobile phones all grew from that insight.
Faraday became famous. He also found that a closed metal cage shields whatever is inside from electric charge.
Which is why we still call it a Faraday cage. It's why you're safe inside a car or a plane in a thunderstorm.
He started the Royal Institution's Christmas Lectures for young people, which still run today.
But he turned down a knighthood. And twice, he refused to become President of the Royal Society.
He said he wanted to remain plain Michael Faraday, to the last.
He was deeply religious, and in the eighteen fifties he refused to help the British government develop poison gas for the Crimean War.
Faraday died in eighteen sixty seven.
A few years later, Thomas Edison and others used generators built on his principle to light up whole streets.
The unit of electrical capacitance, the farad, is named in his honour.
From nineteen ninety one to two thousand and one, his portrait was on the British twenty pound note.
And Albert Einstein kept a picture of Faraday on his study wall, alongside Isaac Newton and James Clerk Maxwell.
He didn't discover electricity. Nobody did.
But Michael Faraday discovered how to make it, how to move it, and how to think about it.
So the next time you flip a switch, remember the bookbinder's boy, with a magnet and a coil of wire.
